questions.question: Describe where the world's hot deserts are found, naming at least four.
questions.expected_answer: Most hot deserts lie in two bands roughly along the Tropic of Cancer and the Tropic of Capricorn, about fifteen to thirty degrees north and south of the equator, often on the western sides of continents. Examples are the Sahara in North Africa, the Arabian Desert, the Thar Desert, the Namib in Namibia, the Kalahari semi-desert, the Australian deserts and the Atacama in Chile.

questions.question: Explain four reasons why hot deserts form.
questions.expected_answer: Air that rose at the equator sinks near the tropics, warming and drying, so clouds cannot form. Cold ocean currents, such as the Benguela Current, cool the air so it does not rise to form rain clouds. Some deserts lie in a rain shadow behind high mountains. Others are very far from the sea, so the winds have lost their moisture before reaching them.

questions.question: Describe the climate of a hot desert and explain why desert nights are cold.
questions.expected_answer: Hot deserts get less than two hundred and fifty millimetres of rain a year, and the rain is rare and irregular, sometimes falling in sudden storms that cause flash floods. Days are very hot, often over forty degrees in summer. Nights can be cold because there are few clouds, so the heat that reached the ground during the day escapes quickly into the clear sky at night, giving a large daily temperature range.
